title: The Solid State
description: The Solid State — Class 12 Chemistry (NCERT): crystalline vs amorphous solids, unit cells, close packing, voids, packing efficiency, density, point defects and properties.

topics.title: Crystalline Solids & Unit Cells
topics.concept:
A solid is the state of matter in which constituent particles are held in fixed positions by strong intermolecular or interionic forces, giving it a definite shape, volume and high density. Solids are broadly classified into two types based on how their particles are arranged.

Crystalline solids have a long-range, regular and repeating arrangement of particles. They are anisotropic (physical properties such as refractive index and electrical conductivity differ with direction), have sharp melting points, definite geometry, and are true solids. Examples: NaCl, diamond, quartz, ice, metals. Amorphous solids (Greek amorphos = no form) have only short-range order, are isotropic, soften over a range of temperature, lack a sharp melting point, and are regarded as supercooled liquids or pseudo-solids. Examples: glass, rubber, plastics.

Crystalline solids are further classified by the nature of the binding force and the particles occupying the lattice points:

  • Ionic solids — ions held by electrostatic force; hard, brittle, high melting, conduct only when molten/aqueous (NaCl, ZnS).
  • Covalent (network) solids — atoms in a continuous covalent network; very hard, very high melting, insulators except graphite (diamond, $\text{SiO}_2$).
  • Molecular solids — molecules held by van der Waals, dipole or hydrogen bonds; soft, low melting, non-conducting ($\text{I}_2$, dry ice $\text{CO}_2$, ice).
  • Metallic solids — kernels in a sea of delocalised electrons; malleable, ductile, lustrous, good conductors (Cu, Fe, Mg).

The orderly three-dimensional arrangement of points representing particle positions is the crystal lattice (space lattice); each point is a lattice point. The smallest repeating portion that, on translation in three dimensions, generates the whole lattice is the unit cell. A unit cell is described by three edge lengths $a,b,c$ and three angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ between them. There are 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices.

Unit cells are either primitive (simple) — particles only at the eight corners — or centred — having additional particles. Centred cells include body-centred (bcc) (one extra particle at the centre of the body), face-centred (fcc/ccp) (one extra at the centre of each of the six faces) and end-centred (one extra at the centre of two opposite faces).

Each particle is shared between adjoining cells, so we count fractional contributions: a corner contributes $\tfrac{1}{8}$ (shared by 8 cells), a face $\tfrac{1}{2}$ (2 cells), an edge $\tfrac{1}{4}$ (4 cells), and a body-centre $1$ (one cell). Hence $z$ per unit cell is: simple cubic $z=8\times\tfrac{1}{8}=1$; bcc $z=8\times\tfrac{1}{8}+1=2$; fcc $z=8\times\tfrac{1}{8}+6\times\tfrac{1}{2}=4$.

examples.problem: How many atoms belong to a simple (primitive) cubic unit cell? Show the counting.
examples.solution:
1. In a simple cubic cell, atoms sit only at the 8 corners.
  2. Each corner atom is shared by 8 unit cells, contributing $\tfrac{1}{8}$.
  3. $z=8\times\tfrac{1}{8}=1$.

Answer: $z=1$ atom per unit cell.

examples.problem: Calculate the number of atoms in a body-centred cubic (bcc) unit cell.
examples.solution:
1. Corners: 8 atoms each contributing $\tfrac{1}{8}$ give $8\times\tfrac{1}{8}=1$.
  2. Body centre: 1 atom belonging entirely to the cell gives $1$.
  3. $z=1+1=2$.

Answer: $z=2$ atoms per unit cell.

examples.problem: Calculate the number of atoms in a face-centred cubic (fcc) unit cell.
examples.solution:
1. Corners: $8\times\tfrac{1}{8}=1$.
  2. Face centres: 6 faces, each face atom shared by 2 cells, $6\times\tfrac{1}{2}=3$.
  3. $z=1+3=4$.

Answer: $z=4$ atoms per unit cell.

examples.problem: An ionic compound has anions A forming the fcc lattice and cations B occupying all the body-centre + edge-centre positions. How many of each ion are present per unit cell?
examples.solution:
1. Anions A (fcc): corners $8\times\tfrac{1}{8}=1$ plus faces $6\times\tfrac{1}{2}=3$, total $A=4$.
  2. Cations B at the body centre: $1\times1=1$.
  3. Cations B at the 12 edge centres: $12\times\tfrac{1}{4}=3$, so $B=1+3=4$.
  4. Formula ratio $A:B=4:4=1:1$, i.e. AB.

Answer: 4 A and 4 B per cell; formula AB.

examples.problem: Why are crystalline solids anisotropic while amorphous solids are isotropic?
examples.solution:
1. In a crystal the arrangement of particles differs along different directions.
  2. So a property measured (e.g. refractive index, conductivity) depends on the direction of measurement — this is anisotropy.
  3. Amorphous solids have a random, irregular arrangement that is statistically the same in all directions, so properties are identical in every direction — isotropy.

Answer: Anisotropy arises from directional regularity in crystals; isotropy from the random arrangement in amorphous solids.

examples.problem: Classify each as ionic, covalent, molecular or metallic: (a) diamond, (b) NaCl, (c) dry ice ($\text{CO}_2$), (d) copper.
examples.solution:
1. Diamond — a continuous network of C–C covalent bonds, so covalent (network) solid.
  2. NaCl — $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ held by electrostatic force, so ionic solid.
  3. Dry ice — discrete $\text{CO}_2$ molecules held by weak van der Waals forces, so molecular solid.
  4. Copper — metal kernels in a sea of delocalised electrons, so metallic solid.

Answer: (a) covalent, (b) ionic, (c) molecular, (d) metallic.

recap: Crystalline solids have long-range order, are anisotropic and melt sharply; amorphous solids have short-range order, are isotropic and soften over a range (pseudo-solids).
Crystalline solids are ionic, covalent (network), molecular or metallic, differing in binding force, hardness, melting point and conductivity.
A crystal lattice is a 3-D array of points; the smallest repeating part is the unit cell, defined by $a,b,c$ and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ (7 systems, 14 Bravais lattices).
Unit cells are primitive (corners only) or centred (bcc, fcc, end-centred).
Contributions: corner $\tfrac{1}{8}$, face $\tfrac{1}{2}$, edge $\tfrac{1}{4}$, body $1$ — giving $z=1$ (simple), $z=2$ (bcc), $z=4$ (fcc).

quiz.q: Which of the following is an amorphous solid?
quiz.explanation: Glass has only short-range order, no sharp melting point, and is isotropic — it is an amorphous (pseudo-) solid.

quiz.q: The number of atoms in a face-centred cubic unit cell is:
A particle present at the centre of an edge is shared by how many unit cells?
quiz.explanation: An edge is shared by 4 unit cells, so an edge particle contributes $\tfrac{1}{4}$ to each.

quiz.q: Diamond is an example of a:
quiz.explanation: In diamond each carbon is covalently bonded to four others forming a giant 3-D network — a covalent (network) solid.

topics.title: Packing, Density & Voids
topics.concept:
To understand how particles fill space we treat them as identical hard spheres and arrange them as compactly as possible — close packing. In a single layer (layer A) each sphere touches six neighbours, giving the maximum two-dimensional packing (hexagonal close packing of one layer).

Stacking layers leads to two important three-dimensional patterns:

  • Hexagonal close packing (hcp) — the third layer lies directly above the first, giving the repeating sequence ABAB... (e.g. Mg, Zn).
  • Cubic close packing (ccp), identical to face-centred cubic (fcc) — the third layer occupies new positions, giving the sequence ABCABC... (e.g. Cu, Ag, Au).

Both hcp and ccp give the same maximum coordination number of 12 (the number of nearest neighbours touching a given sphere) and the same packing efficiency of 74%. A bcc structure has coordination number 8 and a simple cubic structure has coordination number 6.

The empty spaces left between packed spheres are voids (interstitial sites). There are two kinds: a tetrahedral void is surrounded by 4 spheres (smaller, radius ratio $r/R=0.225$) and an octahedral void is surrounded by 6 spheres (larger, $r/R=0.414$). For $N$ close-packed spheres there are $2N$ tetrahedral voids and $N$ octahedral voids.

Packing efficiency is the percentage of total space actually occupied by spheres: $$\text{Packing efficiency}=\frac{z\times\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{a^3}\times100$$ Using the edge–radius relations:

  • Simple cubic: $a=2r$ gives 52.4%.
  • Body-centred cubic: $\sqrt{3}\,a=4r$ gives 68%.
  • Face-centred (ccp) / hcp: $\sqrt{2}\,a=4r$ gives 74% — the most efficient.

Finally, the density of a unit cell connects the microscopic structure to a measurable bulk property:

$$d=\frac{z\,M}{a^3\,N_A}$$ where $z$ = number of atoms (formula units) per unit cell, $M$ = molar mass, $a$ = edge length and $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$ is Avogadro's number. When $a$ is in cm and $M$ in g/mol, $d$ comes out in $\text{g cm}^{-3}$. This single relation lets us find any one of $d,z,M,a$ when the other three are known, and is the workhorse of all numerical problems in this chapter.

examples.problem: A metal crystallises in a face-centred cubic lattice with edge length $a=400\ \text{pm}$ and atomic radius $r$. Find $r$.
examples.solution:
1. For fcc, atoms touch along the face diagonal: $\sqrt{2}\,a=4r$.
  2. $r=\frac{\sqrt{2}\,a}{4}=\frac{1.414\times400}{4}$ pm.
  3. $r=\frac{565.6}{4}=141.4\ \text{pm}$.

Answer: $r\approx141.4\ \text{pm}$.

examples.problem: Show that the packing efficiency of a simple cubic structure is 52.4%.
examples.solution:
1. Simple cubic has $z=1$ and atoms touch along the edge: $a=2r$.
  2. Efficiency $=\frac{1\times\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{a^3}=\frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{(2r)^3}=\frac{\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{8r^3}$.
  3. $=\frac{\pi}{6}=0.524$.
  4. $\times100=52.4\%$.

Answer: 52.4%.

examples.problem: Show that the packing efficiency of a bcc structure is 68%.
examples.solution:
1. For bcc, $z=2$ and atoms touch along the body diagonal: $\sqrt{3}\,a=4r$, so $r=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a$.
  2. Efficiency $=\frac{2\times\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3}{a^3}$. Substitute $r=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a$.
  3. $r^3=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{64}a^3$, so numerator $=2\times\frac{4}{3}\pi\times\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{64}a^3=\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8}a^3$.
  4. Efficiency $=\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi}{8}=0.680=68\%$.

Answer: 68%.

examples.problem: An element (atomic mass $M=56\ \text{g/mol}$) crystallises in bcc with edge $a=2.86\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}$. Find its density. ($N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$)
examples.solution:
1. Use $d=\frac{zM}{a^3 N_A}$ with $z=2$ (bcc).
  2. $a^3=(2.86\times10^{-8})^3=2.34\times10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$.
  3. $d=\frac{2\times56}{(2.34\times10^{-23})(6.022\times10^{23})}=\frac{112}{14.09}$.
  4. $d\approx7.95\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$.

Answer: $d\approx7.95\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ (this is iron).

examples.problem: In a close-packed structure of 0.5 mol of spheres, how many tetrahedral and octahedral voids are present?
examples.solution:
1. Number of spheres $N=0.5\times6.022\times10^{23}=3.011\times10^{23}$.
  2. Octahedral voids $=N=3.011\times10^{23}$.
  3. Tetrahedral voids $=2N=6.022\times10^{23}$.

Answer: $3.011\times10^{23}$ octahedral and $6.022\times10^{23}$ tetrahedral voids.

examples.problem: A face-centred cubic metal has density $d=8.92\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ and molar mass $M=63.5\ \text{g/mol}$. Find the edge length $a$. ($N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$)
examples.solution:
1. Rearrange $d=\frac{zM}{a^3 N_A}$ to $a^3=\frac{zM}{d\,N_A}$ with $z=4$.
  2. $a^3=\frac{4\times63.5}{8.92\times6.022\times10^{23}}=\frac{254}{5.372\times10^{24}}$.
  3. $a^3=4.728\times10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$, so $a=(4.728\times10^{-23})^{1/3}$.
  4. $a\approx3.61\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}=361\ \text{pm}$.

Answer: $a\approx361\ \text{pm}$ (this is copper).

recap: Close packing gives hcp (ABAB...) and ccp/fcc (ABCABC...), both with coordination number 12 and 74% packing efficiency.
For $N$ spheres there are $2N$ tetrahedral voids ($r/R=0.225$) and $N$ octahedral voids ($r/R=0.414$).
Packing efficiency: simple cubic 52.4% ($a=2r$), bcc 68% ($\sqrt{3}a=4r$), fcc/ccp 74% ($\sqrt{2}a=4r$).
Coordination numbers: simple cubic 6, bcc 8, fcc/hcp 12.
Density of a unit cell $d=\frac{zM}{a^3 N_A}$ links $z$, molar mass, edge length and $N_A$ to bulk density.

quiz.q: The packing efficiency of a face-centred cubic (ccp) structure is:
quiz.explanation: Both ccp/fcc and hcp pack spheres most efficiently, occupying 74% of space.

quiz.q: For $N$ close-packed spheres, the number of octahedral voids is:
quiz.explanation: There are $N$ octahedral voids and $2N$ tetrahedral voids for $N$ spheres.

quiz.q: In a body-centred cubic lattice, atoms touch along the:
quiz.explanation: In bcc the corner and body-centre atoms touch along the body diagonal, so $\sqrt{3}\,a=4r$.

quiz.q: The coordination number of an atom in a simple cubic lattice is:
quiz.explanation: Each atom in a simple cubic lattice has 6 nearest neighbours, so the coordination number is 6.

topics.title: Imperfections & Properties
topics.concept:
No real crystal is perfect. Irregularities from the ideal arrangement are called crystal defects or imperfections; when they involve only individual lattice points they are point defects. These defects control colour, conductivity and many useful properties.

In stoichiometric defects the ratio of cations to anions (and hence the chemical formula) stays unchanged. The two main types are:

  • Schottky defect — equal numbers of cations and anions are missing (a vacancy defect). It lowers density and appears in ionic solids with high coordination number and similar-sized ions (NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr).
  • Frenkel defect — a smaller ion (usually the cation) shifts to an interstitial site (a dislocation defect). Density is unchanged; it occurs with a large ion-size difference (ZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI). AgBr shows both.

Non-stoichiometric defects change the cation:anion ratio. A metal excess defect arises when anion sites are vacant and balancing electrons are trapped there, forming F-centres that impart colour (NaCl heated in Na vapour turns yellow; LiCl turns pink). A metal deficiency defect occurs when some cations are missing and the charge is balanced by an ion in a higher oxidation state (e.g. $\text{Fe}_{0.95}\text{O}$, where some $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ becomes $\text{Fe}^{3+}$). Impurity defects arise when foreign ions occupy lattice sites; e.g. $\text{SrCl}_2$ added to NaCl introduces $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ replacing two $\text{Na}^+$, creating cation vacancies.

Electrical properties. Solids span an enormous conductivity range. Conductors (metals) have conductivity $\sim10^7\ \Omega^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}$ because the conduction band overlaps the valence band. Insulators have a very large band gap. Semiconductors have a small band gap, so conductivity rises with temperature. Doping a Group-14 element (Si, Ge) produces:

  • n-type semiconductor — doped with a Group-15 element (P, As); the extra electron carries the current (negative carriers).
  • p-type semiconductor — doped with a Group-13 element (B, Al, Ga); an electron-deficient hole acts as a positive carrier.

Magnetic properties depend on unpaired electrons. Diamagnetic (all electrons paired) are weakly repelled (NaCl, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$); paramagnetic (unpaired electrons) are weakly attracted and lose magnetism when the field is removed ($\text{O}_2$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$). Ferromagnetic solids (Fe, Co, Ni, $\text{CrO}_2$) are strongly attracted and retain magnetism — their domains align in the same direction. Ferrimagnetic solids ($\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4$) have unequal opposite domain alignment (small net moment), while antiferromagnetic solids (MnO) have equal opposite alignment that cancels to zero net moment.

examples.problem: Which point defect lowers the density of an ionic crystal, and why?
examples.solution:
1. In a Schottky defect equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their sites.
  2. The number of ions (mass) decreases while the volume stays the same.
  3. Therefore density (mass/volume) decreases.

Answer: The Schottky defect lowers density because ions are removed without changing the volume.

examples.problem: Why does the Frenkel defect not change the density of a crystal?
examples.solution:
1. In a Frenkel defect an ion only moves from its lattice site to an interstitial site.
  2. No ion leaves the crystal, so total mass is unchanged.
  3. The volume is unchanged, so density stays the same.

Answer: Because the ion is merely displaced (not removed), mass and volume are unchanged, so density is constant.

examples.problem: Explain how an F-centre gives colour to NaCl.
examples.solution:
1. Heating NaCl in sodium vapour creates anion ($\text{Cl}^-$) vacancies (metal excess defect).
  2. Electrons released by extra Na atoms occupy these anion vacancies, forming F-centres.
  3. These trapped electrons absorb visible light and get excited, imparting a yellow colour to the crystal.

Answer: Electrons trapped in anion vacancies (F-centres) absorb visible light, colouring NaCl yellow.

examples.problem: Silicon is doped with phosphorus. What type of semiconductor forms and what carries the current?
examples.solution:
1. Si is a Group-14 element with 4 valence electrons; P is Group-15 with 5.
  2. Four of P's electrons bond with Si; the fifth is free.
  3. This extra (negative) electron carries the current, so an n-type semiconductor forms.

Answer: An n-type semiconductor; the extra free electron is the current carrier.

examples.problem: Classify as diamagnetic, paramagnetic or ferromagnetic: (a) $\text{O}_2$, (b) NaCl, (c) Fe.
examples.solution:
1. $\text{O}_2$ has unpaired electrons, so it is paramagnetic.
  2. NaCl has all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic.
  3. Iron has aligned domains and is strongly attracted, so it is ferromagnetic.

Answer: (a) paramagnetic, (b) diamagnetic, (c) ferromagnetic.

examples.problem: When $\text{SrCl}_2$ is added to NaCl, why are cation vacancies created?
examples.solution:
1. $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ carries two positive charges while $\text{Na}^+$ carries one.
  2. Each $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ replaces two $\text{Na}^+$ to maintain electrical neutrality.
  3. $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ occupies one $\text{Na}^+$ site; the other $\text{Na}^+$ site is left vacant — a cation vacancy.

Answer: One $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ replaces two $\text{Na}^+$, leaving one cation vacancy per added $\text{Sr}^{2+}$.

recap: Stoichiometric defects keep the formula: Schottky (cation + anion vacancies, density falls) and Frenkel (ion in interstitial site, density unchanged).

Non-stoichiometric: metal excess (anion vacancy + trapped electron = F-centre, gives colour) and metal deficiency (missing cation balanced by a higher-oxidation-state ion, e.g. $\text{Fe}_{0.95}\text{O}$).
Impurity defect: a higher-valent ion (e.g. $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ in NaCl) replaces two cations, creating cation vacancies.
Semiconductors: n-type (doped with Group 15, electron carriers); p-type (doped with Group 13, hole carriers).

Magnetism by unpaired electrons: diamagnetic (repelled), paramagnetic (weakly attracted), ferromagnetic (strong, retained), ferrimagnetic (unequal opposite, small net), antiferromagnetic (equal opposite, zero net).

quiz.q: Which defect decreases the density of an ionic solid?
quiz.explanation: In a Schottky defect equal cations and anions are missing, reducing mass and hence density.

quiz.q: An n-type semiconductor is obtained when silicon is doped with:
quiz.explanation: A Group-15 dopant such as P provides an extra electron, giving negative (n-type) charge carriers.

quiz.q: $\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4$ (magnetite) is an example of a substance that is:
quiz.explanation: In $\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4$ the domains align in unequal opposite numbers, giving a net moment — it is ferrimagnetic.

quiz.q: F-centres in a crystal are responsible for:
quiz.explanation: F-centres are electrons trapped in anion vacancies; they absorb visible light and impart colour to the crystal.

questions.q: Amorphous solids are best described as:
questions.explanation: Amorphous solids have only short-range order and flow very slowly, so they are regarded as supercooled liquids or pseudo-solids.

questions.q: The number of atoms per unit cell in a body-centred cubic lattice is:
The packing efficiency of a simple cubic structure is:
questions.explanation: With $a=2r$ and $z=1$, efficiency $=\frac{\pi}{6}=52.4\%$.

questions.q: Both hcp and ccp have a coordination number of:
questions.explanation: In the closest packings each sphere touches 12 neighbours.

questions.q: For $N$ close-packed atoms, the number of tetrahedral voids is:
questions.explanation: There are $2N$ tetrahedral voids and $N$ octahedral voids.

questions.q: The density of a unit cell is given by:
questions.explanation: $d=\frac{zM}{a^3 N_A}$ where $z$ is atoms per cell, $M$ molar mass, $a$ edge length.

questions.q: The Schottky defect causes the density of a crystal to:
questions.explanation: Equal numbers of cations and anions are removed, lowering the mass and hence the density.

questions.q: Which defect is shown by ZnS and AgBr due to the large size difference of ions?
questions.explanation: The small cation occupies an interstitial site — a Frenkel defect — favoured by a large ion-size difference.

questions.q: A face-centred cubic cell has atoms touching along the:
questions.explanation: In fcc, atoms touch along the face diagonal, giving $\sqrt{2}\,a=4r$.

questions.q: An n-type semiconductor is produced by doping silicon with:
questions.explanation: Arsenic (Group 15) donates an extra electron, giving negative (n-type) carriers.

questions.q: The total number of crystal systems and Bravais lattices respectively is:
questions.explanation: There are 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices.

questions.q: Colour in NaCl crystals heated in sodium vapour is due to:
questions.explanation: Electrons trapped in anion vacancies (F-centres) absorb visible light, colouring the crystal yellow.

questions.q: Which of the following is a covalent (network) solid?
questions.explanation: $\text{SiC}$ is held together by a continuous covalent network, like diamond.

questions.q: A particle at the face centre of a unit cell is shared by:
questions.explanation: A face is shared by 2 unit cells, so a face particle contributes $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: $\text{O}_2$ is attracted weakly by a magnetic field. It is therefore:
questions.explanation: $\text{O}_2$ has unpaired electrons and is weakly attracted, so it is paramagnetic.

questions.q: A metal (M = 56 g/mol) crystallises in bcc with $a=2.86\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}$. Its approximate density is:
questions.explanation: $d=\frac{2\times56}{(2.86\times10^{-8})^3\times6.022\times10^{23}}\approx7.9\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$.

questions.q: The radius ratio $r/R$ for a tetrahedral void is:
questions.explanation: A tetrahedral void (4 surrounding spheres) has a limiting radius ratio of 0.225.

questions.q: Antiferromagnetic substances such as MnO have a net magnetic moment of:
questions.explanation: Equal and oppositely aligned domains cancel exactly, giving zero net magnetic moment.

questions.q: When $\text{SrCl}_2$ is added to NaCl, the number of cation vacancies created per $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ ion is:
questions.explanation: One $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ replaces two $\text{Na}^+$; it occupies one site and leaves one cation vacancy.

questions.q: The most efficient packing of identical spheres occupies what fraction of space?
questions.explanation: Both ccp/fcc and hcp achieve the maximum packing efficiency of 74%.

imo.title: The Solid State — IMO / Olympiad Test

questions.q: An element crystallises in fcc with edge $a$. The relation between the atomic radius $r$ and $a$ is:
questions.explanation: fcc: $\sqrt{2}\,a=4r\Rightarrow r=\frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}$.

questions.q: A solid AB has B atoms in ccp and A atoms in all the octahedral voids. The formula and coordination of A is:
questions.explanation: Octahedral voids $=N$ = number of B atoms, so A:B $=1:1$ (AB) and each A sits in an octahedral hole (6-coordinate).

questions.q: A bcc metal has $a=3.0\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}$ and density $5.0\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$. Its molar mass (approx) is:
questions.explanation: $M=\frac{d a^3 N_A}{z}=\frac{5.0\times(2.7\times10^{-23})\times6.022\times10^{23}}{2}\approx41\ \text{g/mol}$.

questions.q: If the radius of an octahedral void is $r$ and that of the close-packed sphere is $R$, then the limiting value of $r/R$ is:
questions.explanation: The geometry of six spheres around a void gives the limiting ratio $r/R=0.414$.

questions.q: In a ccp lattice of N atoms, the total number of voids (tetrahedral + octahedral) is:
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral $=2N$ and octahedral $=N$, giving $3N$ in total.

questions.q: A compound has the formula $\text{M}_x\text{N}$ where N forms ccp and M occupies all tetrahedral voids. Then $x$ equals:
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral voids $=2N$ atoms, so M:N $=2:1$ and $x=2$ (formula $\text{M}_2\text{N}$).

questions.q: On heating, the conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor:
questions.explanation: More electrons gain enough energy to cross the small band gap, so conductivity increases with temperature.

questions.q: The ratio of packing efficiencies of fcc to bcc is closest to:
AgBr can show:
questions.explanation: AgBr is a classic example that exhibits both Schottky and Frenkel defects.

questions.q: The number of nearest neighbours (coordination number) of an atom in a bcc lattice is:
questions.explanation: The body-centre atom touches the 8 corner atoms, so the coordination number is 8.

questions.q: A metal deficiency defect such as $\text{Fe}_{0.95}\text{O}$ is balanced by:
questions.explanation: Missing $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ cations are charge-balanced by converting some $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.

questions.q: A face-centred cubic metal has edge $a=361\ \text{pm}$. Its atomic radius is approximately:
questions.explanation: $r=\frac{a}{2\sqrt{2}}=\frac{361}{2.828}\approx128\ \text{pm}$.

questions.q: Which arrangement gives the lowest packing efficiency?
questions.explanation: Simple cubic occupies only 52.4% of space, the lowest among these.
